title: The serpent (Genesis 3:1–7)
hookLine: did God really say, and the fruit that looked good
last: BONE OF MY BONES, FLESH OF MY FLESH.

lines: A TREE, A WOMAN, A RED APPLE.
cards: Plenty of paintings of this scene share the same props: a tree, a woman reaching up, a shiny red apple, maybe a snake curled around a branch, with a face. Open Genesis and look for the apple. It isn't there.
The text just says fruit. Some readers think the apple grew later, in art, perhaps helped along by a Latin pun: malum means evil, and malum also means apple. The real story is quieter and stranger.
It doesn't start with a bite. It starts with a question.

teach.h: A QUESTION THAT SHRINKS THE GIFT.
teach.b: The serpent, Genesis says, was more subtle than any of the beasts, and its first words are a question. In the Douay-Rheims: "Why hath God commanded you, that you should not eat of every tree of paradise?"
Other translations put it more sharply: did God really say? God had said they could eat of every tree but one. The serpent turns the one limit into the whole story.
The woman corrects it, but now the doubt is in the air. Then the serpent goes further: you won't die; God knows that you'll be like gods. That's the shape of temptation the Church sees here.
First, a question that shrinks the gift and enlarges the rule.
Then the suspicion: maybe God is holding out on you. Then the look.

teach.h: IT LOOKS GOOD TO THE EYES.
teach.b: The tree is good to eat, fair to the eyes, desirable for wisdom. In the story, the wrong choice shows up looking good. She eats, gives some to her husband, who is with her, and he eats.
Their eyes are opened, but all they see is that they're naked. They sew fig leaves.
The Catechism reads this as the first sin: letting trust in God die in the heart, and wanting to be like God without God.
It uses figurative language, the Catechism says, but it tells of a real event at the start of human history. Genesis never names the serpent.
Later scripture fills that in: the Book of Wisdom says death came into the world by the envy of the devil, and Revelation calls the devil that old serpent.

how: Catholics pray "lead us not into temptation" in every Our Father, and the Church reads Genesis 3 on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, as Lent begins.

games.q: you're in the garden. a voice asks why God won't let you eat of every tree. you know you can eat of all but one. what happens in the story?
o: the woman ignores the question and walks away.
the woman corrects it, but the doubt stays, and she looks again at the tree.
games.why: she corrects the serpent, but the question has done its work. she sees the fruit is good to eat and fair to the eyes, and eats, and gives to her husband.

practice: Think of something small you keep doing that you'd rather not: the third episode, the snapped reply, the extra purchase, the scroll at midnight.
Listen for the sentence that comes right before it, usually reasonable, you deserve this, it doesn't really matter, nobody will know, and hear it without arguing back; notice how gentle it sounds.
If you pray, ask for help to recognize it next time.

wordCard.voice: Temptation. Being drawn toward a wrong that looks good. In the garden it starts with a question that makes the gift look small and the limit look huge.
